_meta.title: ServiceNow rapid-learning knowledge base
rules: Every breadcrumb here is a STARTING POINT, not a guarantee. Menu labels move between releases and with which plugins are installed.
Any entry with "confidence": "verify" must be confirmed on your own instance with scripts/sn_probe.js before you teach it to anyone.
Field mandatory-ness is instance-specific: admins add UI policies and dictionary overrides. The probe reads sys_dictionary and reports what YOUR instance actually enforces.

modules.name: Platform basics (Module 0 — do this first)
modules.why: Every other module is the same machinery with different tables. Learn the machinery once and each new module costs you about an hour instead of a week.
breadcrumbs: Filter navigator (top-left, type-anywhere) — your real navigation, faster than clicking menus
All > System Definition > Tables & Columns  (sys_db_object + sys_dictionary: the map of everything)
All > System Definition > Application Menus  (sys_app_module: why a menu item exists / where it points)
All > System Applications > All Available Applications  (what is installed, and what is available to install)
All > User Administration > Users  (sys_user: impersonate a persona to see their menus)
Profile avatar (top-right) > Impersonate user  (the single most useful learning tool on the platform)

guided_setup.note: Platform itself has no guided setup; each application ships its own (see other modules).

flows: Flow Designer: All > Process Automation > Flow Designer
playbooks: All > Process Automation > Process Automation Designer
integrations: IntegrationHub spokes: All > Process Automation > Integrations (per-spoke modules appear after install)
metrics: Platform Analytics: All > Platform Analytics (release-dependent label; older: Performance Analytics)

critical.why: Login id; impersonation and approvals hinge on it.
Inactive users still resolve in history but cannot log in; never delete, deactivate.
Assignment groups are the unit of routing in every ITSM table.
The real answer to 'which fields are required' — read it, do not guess.

must_know: A record is a row; a field is a column; a table extends another table (incident extends task, which extends sys_...base).
Lists are filtered views of a table; a form is one record; a related list is another table filtered to this record.
Almost everything you see is a record in a table. 'Where does this come from?' is answered by Tables & Columns, not by memory.
Dev → Test → Prod is a promotion path, not three copies of your homework. Never experiment in prod.
mistakes: Learning by clicking menus instead of the filter navigator (10x slower, and you never learn the table name).
Skipping impersonation, so you never see the UI the actual user sees.
Assuming your instance looks like the docs screenshot — release + plugins + theme all change it.
quiz: Which table holds the field definitions for the incident table?
How do you find the table behind any list you are looking at?
What is the difference between a role and a group?

modules.name: Incident Management
modules.why: The reference implementation of the whole platform: states, assignment, SLA, notifications, approvals-lite. Learn it and every other process module is a variation.
breadcrumbs: All > Incident > Create New
All > Incident > Open  /  > All  /  > Resolved
All > Incident > Assigned to me  (the only list that matters day one)
Open any incident > right-click the header > Configure > Form Layout (add/remove fields)
Open any incident > Additional actions (⋯) > Create Knowledge (OOB knowledge loop)
All > Service Level Management > SLA Definitions  (what 'SLA' actually means here)

guided_setup.note: ITSM ships guided setup content in recent releases; the menu label and depth differ by release and by whether ITSM Pro is entitled. Confirm with the probe (it lists every module whose name contains 'Guided Setup').

flows: Incident assignment / escalation flows in Flow Designer
Notify on incident comment / state change
playbooks: Incident playbook (Process Automation Designer) on recent releases
Agent Assist / recommended actions inside Service Operations Workspace
dashboards: ITSM / Service Desk dashboard (OOB Performance Analytics content, requires PA)

critical.why: Auto-number; the only identifier users quote. Never edit by hand.
Who is affected. Wrong caller = wrong SLA, wrong comms, wrong reports.
Mandatory by dictionary on OOB; the searchable summary.
Routing. If this is empty, nothing else you configure will get the ticket worked.
Drives SLA pause/resume, close rules, and reporting. Changing state order breaks automation.
These compute priority. Priority is usually derived, not typed.
Enforced at close by OOB UI policy; blank closes corrupt reporting.

useful: u_* custom fields only when a report demands it

must_know: incident extends task. Everything you learn about 'task' fields applies to incident, problem, change, and catalog tasks.
Priority = f(impact, urgency) through a matrix (Data Lookup), not something agents type.
An SLA is a task_sla record attached to the incident; the SLA definition decides start/pause/stop conditions.
Closing requires close_code + close_notes in OOB; that is a UI policy, so it is invisible in the dictionary.
mistakes: Adding a custom field when an unused OOB field already exists.
Editing state choices without checking SLA and flow conditions that reference state values.
Testing as admin only — admin bypasses ACLs, so 'it works' means nothing.
Making assignment_group optional 'to go faster', which silently orphans tickets.
Deleting demo users, which breaks OOB flow references.
quiz: Which fields determine priority, and where is that matrix defined?
What record type implements an SLA on a given incident?
Name three things that break if you reorder state values.

modules.name: Problem + Change Management
modules.why: Where process design lives: approvals, risk, CAB, and the relationship between reactive (problem) and planned (change) work.
breadcrumbs: All > Change > Create New
All > Change > Open  /  > Unassigned  /  > Scheduled
All > Change > Standard Change Catalog  (pre-approved templates — the fastest safe win)
All > Change > Change Advisory Board (CAB) Workbench
All > Problem > Create New
All > Problem > Open  /  > Known Errors

flows: Normal change approval flow (CAB / manager approvals)
playbooks: Change enablement playbook on recent releases
integrations: DevOps: change creation from CI/CD (DevOps Change Velocity)

critical.why: standard / normal / emergency decides which approvals and which fields appear. Get this wrong and approvals never fire.
Mandatory; appears in CAB agenda.
Drives conflict detection and the change calendar.
Routing and approval targeting.
Feed approval policy; changing them mid-flight can re-trigger approvals.
Required by OOB for normal changes; blank plans are the #1 audit finding.

must_know: Standard change = pre-approved via a template; normal goes through CAB; emergency is the 'break glass' path. Choosing the type is the whole design decision.
Approvals are sysapproval_approver records created by a flow, not a field.
A problem is not an incident. Problem = root cause; incident = symptom. Link them, do not merge them.
mistakes: Building approvals with the legacy Workflow Editor when Flow Designer is the supported path on current releases.
Approving as the requester's delegate and calling it a two-person control.
Leaving test_plan blank, then failing an audit.
Creating standard change templates without a retry/backout path.
quiz: Which record type stores an approval?
What makes a change 'standard'?
Where do you configure the change/incident conflict rule?

modules.name: CMDB (and ITOM discovery basics)
modules.why: The CMDB is the platform's spine: incidents, changes, assets, services, and impact analysis all point at CIs. It is also the module people most often 'set up' without understanding.
breadcrumbs: All > Configuration Management Database > CMDB Workspace  (modern UI)
All > Configuration Management Database > CI Class Manager  (class tree, identification rules)
All > Configuration Management > CI Identifiers  (rules that prevent duplicate CIs — set these BEFORE loading data)
All > Configuration Management > Health > CMDB Health Dashboard
All > Discovery > Home  (mid-server / discovery schedules, if ITOM licensed)
All > Configuration Management > CI Relationship Editor

guided_setup.path: All > Configuration Management Database > Guided Setup
guided_setup.note: CMDB guided setup covers identifier rules, health, and data certification. Days-1-5 order matters more than any individual step.

flows: CMDB health scoring jobs (dashboards + scheduled jobs)
integrations: Service Graph Connectors (Import from SCCM, Intune, AWS, Azure, vCenter)

critical.why: Together with the identification rule, decides whether you create a duplicate CI.
You must pick the right class at create time; moving class later is painful.
Impact analysis and asset lifecycle depend on them.
Everything downstream (change risk, alerts) assumes it is right.
Support group routing for CI-related incidents.
Tells you whether a CI is authoritative or hand-typed.

must_know: Identification rules (CI Identifiers) must be configured before you load data, or you ship duplicates on day one.
Relationships are bidirectional records (parent/child); both sides matter for impact analysis.
Class hierarchy is the model: server → linux server → …; put data at the most specific correct class.
CMDB health = correctness + completeness + compliance. Pick one, prove it, then expand.
mistakes: Bulk-importing CIs before defining identification rules (creates thousands of duplicates you cannot merge cleanly).
Using cmdb_ci for everything instead of the proper subclass.
Treating Discovery as 'just install the mid-server' — without credentials and scope, discovery produces noise.
Manually creating CIs that discovery will later duplicate.
quiz: What happens if you load CIs before defining CI identifiers?
Which table stores CI-to-CI relationships?
Name the three components of CMDB health.

modules.name: IT Asset Management (HAM + SAM Pro)
modules.why: Money module: licences, contracts, and hardware lifecycle. Same CI data, different questions ('what do we own, what do we pay, when does it expire').
breadcrumbs: All > Asset > Portfolios > All Assets  (alm_asset)
All > Asset > Assets > Hardware / Software
All > Asset > Contracts > All  (ast_contract)
All > Software Asset Management > License Operations
All > Asset > Asset Lifecycle  (procurement → deploy → retire)

flows: Asset lifecycle flows (request → procure → receive → deploy → retire)
integrations: Service Graph Connectors (Intune/SCCM/Jamf → hardware + software installs)

critical.why: Human key; must be unique and sticker-aligned.
Links asset → model → manufacturer; drives contracts and licences.
Lifecycle truth: on order / in stock / in use / retired.
Custody. Missing owner = lost asset.
Asset and CI must agree or reporting lies.
Renewal alerts and true-up run off these.

must_know: Assets (alm_asset) and CIs (cmdb_ci) are different records that point at each other. One asset can map to one CI; not everything is an asset.
SAM Pro needs the software install data feed (SCCM/Intune/agent) or the license position is fiction.
Licence compliance = rights (entitlement) vs installs/usage; you need both sides.
mistakes: Loading the asset register as CIs, or vice versa.
Assuming SAM works without publisher-specific reconciliation rules.
Ignoring contract renewal dates until the auto-renewal already happened.
quiz: What is the difference between alm_asset and cmdb_ci?
Which table holds licence entitlement?
What reconciles installs against rights?

modules.name: HR Service Delivery (HRSD)
modules.why: The cleanest example of 'same engine, different domain': cases instead of incidents, and confidentiality (ACLs) becomes the whole design.
breadcrumbs: All > HR > Cases > All
All > HR > Employee Center (portal experience)
All > HR > Administration > HR Services  (what the employee can ask for)
All > HR > Administration > HR Profiles
All > HR > Lifecycle Events  (onboarding/offboarding orchestration)

critical.why: The employee the case is about — distinct from the opener. Wrong value leaks or hides data.
Selects the workflow, SLA, and fields. The single most important choice on the form.
HRSD states include work-in-progress/awaiting-info; alert/notification logic keys off them.
Confidentiality depends on the who.
Routing between HR COEs; no group = no service.

must_know: Confidentiality in HRSD is ACLs + restricted fields, not a checkbox. Design it first.
HR Services (not 'categories') are the catalog of what employees can request; each carries its own workflow.
Lifecycle Events orchestrate many cases/tasks across departments (onboarding day 1 ≠ one case).
mistakes: Reusing ITIL assignment groups for HR COEs.
Ignoring confidentiality until after go-live (retrofitting ACLs is a rebuild).
Building one giant 'ask HR' service instead of a catalog.
quiz: Which field drives HRSD workflow selection?
What enforces confidentiality?
What orchestrates onboarding across departments?

modules.name: Security Operations (SecOps)
modules.why: Shows the platform as an integration hub: alerts arrive from tools, correlate into incidents, spawn response tasks and playbooks.
breadcrumbs: All > Security Operations > Security Incidents > All
All > Security Operations > All Alerts
All > Security Operations > Administration > Alert Ingestion (integration profiles)
All > Security Operations > Threat Intelligence (observables, IOC feeds)
All > Security Operations > Security Incident Response Workspace

playbooks: Security incident response playbooks (per incident category)
integrations: Splunk / CrowdStrike / Defender / Palo Alto / Qualys spokes

critical.why: Drives the response playbook and required fields.
Derived from risk/severity; gates escalation.
Tier routing is the SOC operating model.
Investigate → contain → eradicate → recover → review; review cannot be skipped for compliance.
The evidence chain; without them, enrichment and reporting are empty.

must_know: Alerts are not incidents. Correlation rules turn N alerts into 1 incident — that rule set is the product.
Playbooks (Process Automation Designer) are the response backbone; the incident form is just the record.
Observables (IOCs) are child records used for enrichment and threat intel matching.
mistakes: Turning every alert into an incident (alert fatigue plus a useless MTTR).
Skipping post-incident review state to 'close faster', losing compliance evidence.
Loading intel feeds without tuning observables first.
quiz: What turns many alerts into one incident?
Which record holds IOCs?
Which state cannot be skipped?

modules.name: Governance, Risk & Compliance (IRM)
modules.why: Regulator-facing: entities, risks, controls, tests, issues. The data model is the hardest on the platform — do it in the right order or you rebuild.
breadcrumbs: All > GRC > Risk > Risk Register
All > GRC > Compliance > Controls
All > GRC > Compliance > Policies
All > GRC > Audit > Engagements
All > GRC > Administration > Entity Types  (the scoping model — build this first)

critical.why: A risk without an entity is not auditable.
The whole methodology lives in that pair.
Accountability; attestations route to this person.
Compliance claim without evidence fails audit.
Drive escalations and regulatory reporting.

must_know: Build order: entities → risks → controls → tests → issues. Any other order creates orphan data.
IRM tables are the least 'guessable' on the platform; use the guided setup as the curriculum, not the docs.
Scoring matrices are configuration; changing them after assessments exist rewrites your history.
mistakes: Starting with controls instead of entities and risks.
Treating a GRC implementation as a data-entry project (it is a methodology decision).
No evidence attachments — fails audit regardless of perfect status fields.
quiz: What is the correct build order for IRM?
Which pair of scores drives risk reporting?
What makes a control 'tested'?

modules.name: Customer Service Management (CSM)
modules.why: ITSM pointed outward: cases, accounts, entitlements, SLAs against paying customers, and a portal that customers actually use.
breadcrumbs: All > Customer Service > Cases > All
All > Customer Service > Accounts
All > Customer Service > Administration > Entitlements
All > Customer Service > Customer Service Portal (or the CSM Configurable Workspace)
All > Customer Service > Administration > Case types

critical.why: Everything (entitlement, SLA, reporting) hangs off the account.
Who reported it; drives auth and comms.
Decides whether service is included — get it wrong and you bill/deny wrongly.
Selects workflow and required fields.
Contractual, not internal, promise.

must_know: Entitlement checks are the CSM-specific twist; without them SLAs are guesses.
External users are real users with ACLs — test as the customer, not as admin.
Case types are the CSM equivalent of catalog items: they define what an agent can even do.
mistakes: Skipping entitlement setup
Testing the portal as admin
One case type for every request
quiz: What decides if service is included?
Where do customer-visible SLAs come from?
What selects the case workflow?

modules.name: Field Service Management (FSM)
modules.why: Scheduling + mobile work: work orders, tasks, territories, and the constraint engine. The visual (dispatch map) hides a lot of configuration.
breadcrumbs: All > Field Service Management > Work Orders > All
All > Field Service Management > Dispatch > Dispatch Board
All > Field Service Management > Administration > Territories
All > Field Service Management > Administration > Scheduling > Constraints

guided_setup.path: All > Field Service Management > Guided Setup

critical.why: Primary routing constraint; wrong territory = unassignable work.
Drives the whole scheduling engine and customer promise.
Who actually does the work.
Skill matching decides eligibility.
Travel time and dispatch map depend on coordinates.

must_know: Work order = the business ask; task = the visit; assignment = who/when. Three tables, three concepts.
Constraints (skills, territory, hours) are configuration, not code — but bad data makes the engine look broken.
Mobile behaviour must be tested on Now Mobile, not desktop.
mistakes: No territories (then everything is unschedulable)
Skipping skill data
Testing only as dispatcher
quiz: Difference between work order, task, assignment?
What are the three main scheduling constraints?

modules.name: App Engine Studio (build your own app)
modules.why: The fastest way to internalize the platform: build one tiny app end-to-end (table → form → flow → portal/role). One hour here teaches more than three docs.
breadcrumbs: All > App Engine Studio  (guided builder)
All > System Applications > Studio  (classic dev environment)
All > System Definition > Tables  (create table manually)
All > Process Automation > Flow Designer > New > Action/Flow
All > System Definition > Plugins  (install what you need — asks for admin)

guided_setup.note: App Engine Studio is a builder, not a guided setup.

flows: App templates (request app, approvals app, etc.)
playbooks: Playbook templates inside Process Automation Designer
integrations: IntegrationHub actions from the app scope
REST step in Flow Designer (no code)
dashboards: Custom reports on your own table

critical.why: Naming is permanent-ish; renaming later breaks references.
Global vs scoped decides whether you can use OOB tables freely.
Without an app role, everyone is admin or nobody can see it.
Flows and reports key off state; design the states first.

must_know: Scoped app = cannot touch global tables/scripts without explicit cross-scope access. Decide scope before adding tables.
Start from a table, not a form: data model first, then UI, then automation.
Every app should ship with a role; otherwise security is an afterthought.
mistakes: Global scope by default, then wondering why upgrades conflict
No app role
Building UI before the data model
quiz: What does a scope prevent?
What is the first artifact you build?
Where is a scoped app's menu defined?

modules.name: Integration: REST, IntegrationHub, Remote Tables
modules.why: The single highest-leverage skill on the platform. Every 'can ServiceNow do X with our other system' question lands here.
breadcrumbs: All > System Web Services > Outbound > REST Message  (sys_rest_message — call someone else)
All > System Web Services > Scripted REST APIs  (sys_ws_definition — someone calls you)
All > System Web Services > Remote Tables  (expose a REST API AS a table)
All > Process Automation > Flow Designer > Action (REST step, generated action)
All > System OAuth > Application Registry  (credentials for outbound calls)
All > System Logs > Outbound HTTP Requests  (the log nobody checks and everybody needs)

guided_setup.note: No guided setup for generic REST; IntegrationHub spokes do ship guided setup per spoke.

integrations: REST/SOAP/JSON/XML, LDAP, JDBC, email, file, MID Server for on-prem
dashboards: Integration health dashboards (custom, built on sys_outbound_http_log)

critical.why: Half of all integration bugs are wrong URL, method, or content-type.

critical.field: Authentication (basic / OAuth 2.0 / API key in header)
critical.why: Never hardcode secrets; use Connection & Credential aliases.
APIs reject silently-wrong content types.
This is where 'it returned 200 but nothing happened' lives.
Default timeouts make slow APIs look broken.

must_know: Outbound REST Message = ServiceNow calls out. Scripted REST API = the world calls in. Remote Table = the world's API pretends to be a table.
Remote Tables are read-only views. If you need writes, use REST + Flow/scripted action.
Use Connection & Credential aliases so credentials are not in the message body or scripts.
Check sys_outbound_http_log before blaming the API.
mistakes: Hardcoding tokens in scripts (leaks into update sets and logs).
Ignoring the response status: 200-with-error-payload is common.
Not pinning content-type, then debugging JSON parse errors for an hour.
Building a remote table for high-volume joins (performance cliff) instead of a scheduled sync.
quiz: Which table stores an outbound REST message?
When is a Remote Table the wrong tool?
Where do you look first when an outbound call fails?

modules.name: Analytics: metrics, dashboards, Performance Analytics
modules.why: This is how anyone believes your work happened. Learn indicator → breakdown → dashboard once and every module's reporting becomes mechanical.
breadcrumbs: All > Platform Analytics  (newer releases; older: Performance Analytics)
All > Platform Analytics > Indicators  (pa_indicators: what is being measured)
All > Platform Analytics > Breakdowns  (the 'by what' — priority, group, assignment)
All > Platform Analytics > Dashboards / Library
All > Reports > View / Create New  (classic reporting still works and is often enough)
All > Platform Analytics > Data Collector  (scheduled jobs that snapshot scores)

guided_setup.note: There is also an 'Analytics' / PA onboarding checklist on some releases. Probe for modules matching 'Guided Setup'.

flows: OOB PA content packs per module (ITSM, HRSD, CSM, SecOps, CMDB)
playbooks: KPI accelerator workflows (Target/KPI Signals on newer releases)
integrations: Export to Power BI / Tableau via ODBC or scheduled export
metrics: Indicator scores, targets, thresholds, KPI signals, MTTR, SLA %

critical.why: Count/avg of what, filtered how. Vague source = untrustworthy number.
Most 'wrong numbers' are wrong filters, not wrong math.
The 'by' dimension; without it a number cannot drive action.
Daily vs weekly decides whether you see trends or snapshots.
Turns a number into an alert.

must_know: Indicator = what to measure. Breakdown = how to slice it. Dashboard = how to show it. That is the entire model.
PA needs a data collector to keep scores current; nothing is real-time by default.
Analytics visibility (who sees which rows) is separate from ACLs and is a common leak.
Platform Analytics (newer) and Performance Analytics (classic) coexist; don't assume docs match your release.
mistakes: Building 40 indicators instead of 3 that someone will act on.
Reporting on data that is dirty upstream (report the truth, then fix the data).
Forgetting the collector schedule, then wondering why numbers froze.
Publishing dashboards to users who cannot see the underlying rows.
quiz: What are the three parts of the PA model?
What keeps scores up to date?
Why can a correct indicator look wrong?
